samples.description: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
samples.metric: Research preprint · review methods and evidence
samples.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters

samples.description: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.
samples.metric: Research preprint · review methods and evidence
samples.title: SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse

samples.description: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.What AI changes about vulnerability discoveryVulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI lecture, Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey previews this week's tools, Claude Code and Codex, with a three-step process for preparing, generating, and reviewing vibe-coded work. Then she looks past launch: why even a carefully built AI tool needs monitoring, how the NIST AI Risk Management Framework structures responsible AI across a product's life cycle, and what Stanford's Responsible AI guidance asks of you. The lecture closes with evaluation: what you are measuring, and why ground truth is harder to pin down than it looks. Key questions answered in this lecture: Q: What is vibe coding? A: Bailey describes vibe coding as using English as a programming language with AI tools like Claude Code and Codex. Done professionally (some call it agentic engineering) it follows three steps: prepare a detailed spec with the elephant and goldfish process, hand it to a fresh coding agent, then review the result. Q: How can I review vibe-coded work if I can't read code? A: Bailey recommends starting another fresh 'goldfish' agent in a coding environment, giving it your scope of work and the code, and asking it to act as a severe code reviewer. Frame the code as someone else's work that may not follow the spec, to push the AI away from praise. Q: Why do AI systems need monitoring after deployment? A: Bailey says conditions change after deployment: distribution shift, users changing behavior once they know AI is involved (like students adding prompt-injection notes for an AI autograder), and models that update their weights. samples.description: Explore AI courses and programs from Stanford Online: https://stanford.io/4BYTekh What happens when AI stops just writing and starts acting on your behalf? In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI lecture recording, Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey explains how AI agents work and why prompt injection gets much worse once AI can take actions. She opens with connectors, the links that let AI read your email, calendar, or files and act on your behalf, and shows that nothing new is happening inside the model: it's the same next-token prediction behind every chatbot, occasionally generating specially structured text that triggers actions. From there she builds the vocabulary for autonomous work: the analyze, act, observe loop every agent runs on, the seven-part"anatomy"of a well-specified agent, and professional-grade agentic workflow techniques like"the elephant and the goldfish."The lecture closes by putting on a pessimistic security hat: for any agent you design, what's the worst that could happen, and whose permissions made it possible? Key questions answered in this lecture recording: Q: What is the difference between generative AI and agentic AI? A: Bailey says agentic AI focuses on taking actions rather than only generating content, but it runs on the same next-token prediction: the LLM emits structured JSON text that a connector turns into an action. Q: What is an AI connector? A: Connectors are access permissions that plug your AI tool into apps like Gmail or Outlook so it can pull in data or act on your behalf. Enabling one adds tool instructions to the context window, using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Q: What should you include when you define an AI agent? samples.description: A combination of pressure points that question traditional approaches to evaluation is experienced in the Global South and low-density rural higher education contexts. The chapter explores the AI-enabled assessment for the Global South, rural and resource-constrained higher education. It draws together cross-sectional evidence about approaches to architecture, governance, pedagogy and equity in order to explore how AI can support assessment whilst respecting local goals and limitations. The Principal Analysis spots four design levers, namely: lightweight and offline-capable assessment tools; governance and data sovereignty-based data collection; modular architectures through capacity building and evidence across domains. But there will be growing dangers in relation to data privacy, algorithmic bias, inequalities in language and culture, as well as dependency on suppliers. The chapter ends with policy, university governance and sustainable scaling implications focused on learner rights and educational justice that is locally stewarded.
samples.title: AI and Assessment in Global South, Rural, and Resource-Constrained Higher Education Contexts

samples.description: The rapid growth of Generative Artificial Intelligence in higher education has made assessment more complex. Its importance lies in protecting genuine learning and academic integrity in AI rich environments. The main objective of this chapter is to explain how assessment and feedback practices can be redesigned to measure real understanding instead of automated output. The chapter shows that authentic tasks, staged submissions, reflection, and oral interaction improve validity and fairness. Key findings suggest that formative feedback, clear AI guidelines, and process based evaluation strengthen integrity. The chapter concludes that thoughtful redesign helps institutions maintain standards while adapting to technological change.
samples.title: Redesigning Authentic Assessment and Feedback Practices in the Generative AI Era

samples.description: Pigs are important agricultural resources and valuable biomedical models, necessitating a high-quality pan-genome to comprehensively capture genomic diversity. Here we present an extensive genomic and phenotypic resource comprising 3 telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genomes and 16 high-quality assemblies. This resource enables the construction of the pig pan-transcriptome and pan-metabolome, thereby enhancing genotype-phenotype mapping. Using 12 Y-chromosome assemblies, we resolved centromere repositioning at basepair resolution, establishing centromeres as unique evolutionary markers. Reconstruction of centromeric three-dimensional genomic architecture revealed their role as structural scaffolds that concentrate chromatin interactions. We identified eEF1A1, a transcriptionally active gene consistently located near chromosome 1 centromeres, as a candidate hotspot for karyotype variation. From a pan-structural variation map, we pinpointed AKR1B1 as a key gene underlying hypoxia adaptation. Moreover, a graph-based pan-genome built from T2T genomes improved heritability capture. Together, this work provides a foundation for studies of centromere evolution, adaptive genetics and precision breeding.

samples.description: Liquid scintillation counting provides high efficiency for beta emitters, but strongly acidic, alkaline, and saline samples can restrict sample loading and increase blank signals. Polystyrene-based plastic scintillation microspheres (PSm) doped with PPO and bis-MSB were therefore evaluated as a heterogeneous counting medium and compared with OptiPhase HiSafe 3 in representative aqueous matrices. The prepared PSm were spherical, with particle sizes mainly of 110-230 μm. Their response was strongly energy dependent: counting efficiencies were 0.38% for 3H, 40.2% for 14C, and an apparent 184.6% for 90Sr/90Y at secular equilibrium when normalized to 90Sr activity, compared with 41.5%, 93.2%, and 198.9%, respectively, for HiSafe 3. PSm allowed a fixed sample loading ratio of 0.50 mL/g under all tested matrix conditions and exhibited blank count rates of 20.9-28.1 cpm when measured for 10 min after 24 h of dark storage. The operational loading capacity of HiSafe 3 varied from 0.04 to 0.80 mL/mL. Following approximately 24 h of dark storage, its blank count rate reached 246.6 cpm in 4 mol/L NaOH during a 10 min measurement. For 14C, under the standardized conditions of 24 h dark storage and 10 min counting, PSm gave calculated minimum detectable activity concentrations (MDCs) of 138.8-170.2 Bq/L. HiSafe 3 gave lower MDCs for water, 1 mol/L NaOH, and 1 mol/L NaCl, whereas PSm gave lower MDCs in 2-4 mol/L NaOH, all tested HCl matrices, and 2-4 mol/L NaCl, including a 6.8-fold lower MDC in 2 mol/L HCl. Independent quantitative evaluation of the PSm system was limited to water and 1 mol/L HCl, NaOH, and NaCl over 1.8-200 kBq/L, with relative deviations within 11.1%.
